decks.title: Phenols and Ethers — Part 1: Phenols
goals: Classify and name phenols and write equations for preparing phenol by four methods
Explain why phenol is more acidic than ethanol, and write its reactions with NaOH, Na, Zn, acetyl chloride, acetic anhydride and PCl₅
Predict products of electrophilic substitution, Kolbe and Reimer–Tiemann reactions
Describe the ferric chloride and azo dye tests and uses of phenol

slides.heading: Phenols
slides.body_md: Part 1 — compounds with an –OH group directly on a benzene ring.

visual.alt: Table of phenols and their uses

slides.narration: Namaste! Joseph Lister used phenol, then called carbolic acid, to make surgery safe. Today phenol is used to make plastics like Bakelite, aspirin and disinfectants. In phenols the hydroxyl group is joined directly to a benzene ring, and this makes them quite different from alcohols. In this part we see how phenol is made, why it is acidic, and how it reacts.

slides.heading: Classification and nomenclature
slides.body_md: Phenols are **monohydric**, **dihydric** or **trihydric** by the number of –OH groups on the ring. Substituted phenols are named as derivatives of phenol, numbering from the C–OH carbon.

visual.alt: Table of names of phenols

slides.narration: Phenol itself has one hydroxyl group on the ring. The cresols are methylphenols. Benzene diols have two hydroxyl groups: catechol, resorcinol and quinol, with the groups in the one-two, one-three and one-four positions. Pyrogallol has three. In IUPAC names, numbering starts at the carbon carrying the hydroxyl group.

slides.heading: Preparation of phenol
slides.body_md: Four methods: (1) from **benzenediazonium chloride** (warm with water); (2) from **chlorobenzene** (Dow process: NaOH, 623 K, 300 atm); (3) from **benzenesulphonic acid** (sodium salt fused with NaOH, then acid); (4) from **cumene** (industrial).

visual.alt: Table of methods of preparing phenol

slides.narration: Phenol can be made in four ways. A diazonium salt gives phenol simply on warming with water. Chlorobenzene reacts with sodium hydroxide only at high temperature and pressure. Sodium benzenesulphonate is fused with solid sodium hydroxide. In the last three cases sodium phenoxide is formed first, and acid then releases phenol. Industry uses the cumene process.

slides.heading: The cumene process
slides.body_md: Benzene + propene (acid catalyst) → **cumene** (isopropylbenzene); air oxidises it to **cumene hydroperoxide**; dilute acid splits this into **phenol and propanone** (acetone).

visual.alt: Flow of the cumene process

slides.narration: Most phenol is made by the cumene process. Benzene and propene combine to give cumene, which air oxidises to cumene hydroperoxide. Dilute acid then splits the hydroperoxide into phenol and propanone. The process is economical because it uses cheap raw materials and both products are valuable.

slides.heading: Worked example: phenol from benzene
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Convert benzene into phenol by way of benzenesulphonic acid, giving reagents and conditions.

**Step 1.** Sulphonate: $\ce{C6H6 + H2SO4 ->[\Delta] C6H5SO3H + H2O}$ (conc. or fuming H₂SO₄).

**Step 2.** Neutralise: $\ce{C6H5SO3H + NaOH -> C6H5SO3Na + H2O}$.

**Step 3.** Fuse with NaOH at about 573 K: $\ce{C6H5SO3Na + 2NaOH -> C6H5ONa + Na2SO3 + H2O}$.

**Step 4.** Acidify: $\ce{C6H5ONa + HCl -> C6H5OH + NaCl}$.

visual.alt: Table of intermediates from benzene to phenol

slides.narration: Benzene is first heated with concentrated sulphuric acid to give benzenesulphonic acid, which is neutralised to its sodium salt. Fusing this salt with solid sodium hydroxide at about five hundred and seventy three kelvin replaces the sulphonate group by an oxide ion, giving sodium phenoxide and sodium sulphite. Finally, acid releases phenol.

slides.heading: Quick check: preparation
slides.body_md: Identify a method or product in the preparation of phenol.
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember the by-product of the cumene process and the conditions of the Dow process.

slides.heading: Physical properties
slides.body_md: Phenol is a colourless solid (m.p. 316 K) that turns pink in air; it has a characteristic smell and is **corrosive**. Hydrogen bonding gives phenols higher boiling points than arenes or haloarenes of similar mass; phenol is moderately soluble in water. **2-Nitrophenol** has **intramolecular** hydrogen bonding, so it is more volatile and less soluble than 4-nitrophenol (**intermolecular**) and can be steam distilled.

visual.alt: Table of boiling points showing hydrogen bonding effects

slides.narration: Phenol is a colourless crystalline solid that slowly turns pink in air. It burns the skin, so it must be handled with care. Its hydrogen bonds give it a much higher boiling point than toluene of almost the same mass. In two-nitrophenol the hydrogen bond forms inside one molecule, so the molecules are not linked to each other: it is more volatile and can be separated from four-nitrophenol by steam distillation.

slides.heading: Acidity of phenol
slides.body_md: Phenol (pKa 10.0) is about 10⁶ times more acidic than ethanol (pKa 15.9): the **phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance**, the negative charge being delocalised over O and the ortho and para carbons. Electron-withdrawing groups (–NO₂) at o/p increase acidity; electron-donating groups (–CH₃, –OCH₃) decrease it. Phenol dissolves in NaOH but not in NaHCO₃ (weaker than carbonic acid).

slides.narration: When phenol loses a proton, the negative charge on the phenoxide ion spreads into the ring, onto the ortho and para carbons, as these resonance structures show. Spreading the charge stabilises the ion, so phenol is far more acidic than ethanol. Nitro groups at ortho or para positions spread the charge further and increase acidity; methyl and methoxy groups push electrons in and decrease it. Phenol is still weaker than carbonic acid.

slides.heading: Worked example: ranking acidity
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Arrange in increasing acid strength: cyclohexanol, phenol, 3-nitrophenol, 4-methoxyphenol, 2,4,6-trinitrophenol.

**Step 1.** Cyclohexanol (pKa ≈ 16): no resonance in the alkoxide — weakest.

**Step 2.** 4-Methoxyphenol (10.2): –OCH₃ releases electrons, slightly weaker than phenol (10.0).

**Step 3.** 3-Nitrophenol (8.3): –I effect only from meta.

**Step 4.** 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol (≈ 0.4): three o/p nitro groups.

**Order:** cyclohexanol < 4-methoxyphenol < phenol < 3-nitrophenol < 2,4,6-trinitrophenol.

visual.alt: Table of pKa values

slides.narration: Compare the stability of each anion. Cyclohexanol has no ring to delocalise the charge, so it is the weakest acid. A methoxy group pushes electrons into the ring and makes phenoxide slightly less stable. A nitro group at the meta position withdraws electrons only inductively, but three nitro groups at ortho and para positions delocalise the charge so well that picric acid is almost as strong as a mineral acid.

slides.body_md: Compare the acidity of phenols and alcohols.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about resonance in the phenoxide ion and the effect of substituents at ortho and para positions.

slides.heading: Reactions of the –OH group
slides.body_md: Phenol reacts with **NaOH** and **Na** (phenoxide), is reduced by hot **zinc dust** to benzene, and is acylated by **acetyl chloride** or **acetic anhydride** to phenyl ethanoate. With **PCl₅** the yield of chlorobenzene is poor (C–O bond has partial double-bond character); triphenyl phosphate forms instead.

visual.alt: Table of reactions of the –OH group of phenol

slides.narration: Being acidic, phenol dissolves in sodium hydroxide and reacts with sodium, forming sodium phenoxide. Heated with zinc dust, it loses its oxygen and gives benzene. Acetyl chloride or acetic anhydride converts it into the ester phenyl ethanoate. Unlike alcohols, phenol gives only a poor yield of chlorobenzene with phosphorus pentachloride, because its carbon–oxygen bond is strengthened by resonance.

slides.heading: Electrophilic substitution in phenol
slides.body_md: –OH strongly **activates** the ring (+R) and directs **ortho/para**. **Bromine water** → white precipitate of **2,4,6-tribromophenol**; Br₂ in CS₂ (low temperature) → 2- and 4-bromophenol. **Dilute HNO₃** → 2- and 4-nitrophenol; **conc. HNO₃** → picric acid. **Conc. H₂SO₄:** 2-hydroxybenzenesulphonic acid at about 290 K, 4-isomer at about 373 K.

visual.alt: Table of electrophilic substitution of phenol

slides.narration: The hydroxyl group feeds electrons into the ring, so phenol reacts with electrophiles far faster than benzene, at ortho and para positions. In water, bromine gives a white precipitate of tribromophenol at once; in a non-polar solvent at low temperature, only one bromine goes in. Dilute nitric acid gives the nitrophenols, concentrated nitric acid gives picric acid, and sulphonation gives the ortho acid at low temperature and the para acid at high temperature.

slides.heading: Kolbe and Reimer–Tiemann reactions
slides.body_md: **Kolbe:** sodium phenoxide + CO₂ (about 400 K, 4–7 atm), then H⁺ → **salicylic acid** (2-hydroxybenzoic acid). **Reimer–Tiemann:** phenol + CHCl₃ + aqueous NaOH (about 340 K), then H⁺ → **salicylaldehyde** (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde); the electrophile is dichlorocarbene, :CCl₂.

visual.alt: Table of Kolbe and Reimer–Tiemann reactions

slides.narration: Two named reactions add a carbon group at the ortho position. In the Kolbe reaction, sodium phenoxide is heated with carbon dioxide under pressure, and acidification gives salicylic acid, the starting point for aspirin. In the Reimer–Tiemann reaction, phenol is warmed with chloroform and sodium hydroxide; dichlorocarbene attacks the ring, and after hydrolysis and acidification salicylaldehyde is obtained.

slides.heading: Worked example: products of phenol
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Name the main product: (a) phenol + bromine water; (b) phenol + Br₂ in CS₂ at 273 K; (c) sodium phenoxide + CO₂, 400 K, then acid; (d) phenol + CHCl₃/NaOH, then acid; (e) phenol + zinc dust, heat.

**(a)** 2,4,6-Tribromophenol. **(b)** 4-Bromophenol (major) and 2-bromophenol.

**(c)** Salicylic acid. **(d)** Salicylaldehyde. **(e)** Benzene.

visual.alt: Table of products from phenol

slides.narration: In water, bromine is strongly polarised and the phenol partly ionised, so all three activated positions are substituted. In carbon disulphide at low temperature the reaction is milder and gives mainly para-bromophenol. The Kolbe reaction gives salicylic acid and the Reimer–Tiemann reaction gives salicylaldehyde, both with the new group ortho to the hydroxyl. Zinc dust strips off the oxygen to give benzene.

slides.heading: Tests for phenol and uses
slides.body_md: **Ferric chloride test:** neutral FeCl₃ gives a **violet** colour with phenol (alcohols do not). **Azo dye test:** phenol in NaOH couples with benzenediazonium chloride at 273–278 K to give an **orange** dye, 4-hydroxyazobenzene. **Bromine water:** white precipitate. **Uses:** antiseptics and disinfectants, Bakelite (with methanal), salicylic acid and aspirin, picric acid, dyes, nylon intermediates.

visual.alt: Table of tests distinguishing phenol from ethanol

slides.narration: Several simple tests identify phenol. Neutral iron three chloride gives a violet colour. Bromine water gives a white precipitate. In alkaline solution, phenol couples with a cold diazonium salt to form an orange azo dye. Ethanol gives none of these results. Phenol is used to make disinfectants, Bakelite, aspirin and many dyes.

slides.body_md: Predict a product of phenol or choose a test that distinguishes it from an alcohol.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Phenol from diazonium salts, chlorobenzene (Dow), benzenesulphonate fusion, cumene (with propanone).
Acidic (pKa 10): phenoxide resonance; o/p-NO₂ increase, –CH₃/–OCH₃ decrease acidity; dissolves in NaOH, not NaHCO₃.
NaOH, Na → phenoxide; Zn → benzene; CH₃COCl/(CH₃CO)₂O → phenyl ethanoate; PCl₅ poor.
EAS: Br₂(aq) → tribromophenol; nitration; sulphonation; Kolbe → salicylic acid; Reimer–Tiemann → salicylaldehyde.
Tests: FeCl₃ violet; azo dye orange; bromine water white ppt.

visual.alt: Summary table of named reactions

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Phenol is made from diazonium salts, chlorobenzene, benzenesulphonates and, industrially, from cumene. Resonance in the phenoxide ion makes phenol far more acidic than alcohols. The hydroxyl group activates the ring for ortho and para substitution, and the Kolbe and Reimer–Tiemann reactions add carboxyl and aldehyde groups. Phenol is identified with ferric chloride, bromine water and the azo dye test.

Specify solvent for bromination: water (tribromo) vs CS₂ (mono).
Name the products of Kolbe and Reimer–Tiemann and state they are ortho.
For tests, give reagent, observation for phenol and for the other compound.

slides.narration: Some tips. Draw the resonance structures of the phenoxide ion when explaining acidity. State the solvent in bromination. Name the products of the Kolbe and Reimer–Tiemann reactions correctly. And in distinguishing tests, describe what happens with both compounds.

decks.title: Phenols and Ethers — Part 2: Ethers
goals: Describe the structure of the ether group and name ethers
Choose reactants for Williamson’s synthesis of a given ether
Write reactions of ethers with chlorine, oxygen, HI and PCl₅
Write halogenation, nitration and Friedel–Crafts reactions of anisole, and state uses of ethers

slides.heading: Ethers
slides.body_md: Part 2 — R–O–R′: structure, preparation, properties and reactions, including anisole.

visual.alt: Flow of the main ideas about ethers

slides.narration: Ethers contain an oxygen atom joined to two carbon groups. Diethyl ether was one of the first general anaesthetics and is still a common laboratory solvent, and anisole gives some perfumes their smell. In this part we look at the structure and names of ethers, how they are made, their physical properties and their reactions.

slides.heading: Structure and nomenclature
slides.body_md: The ether oxygen is **sp³** with two lone pairs; the C–O–C angle (about 111.7° in methoxymethane) is larger than tetrahedral because the alkyl groups repel. Ethers are **symmetrical** (R–O–R) or **unsymmetrical** (R–O–R′). IUPAC: **alkoxyalkanes**, the larger group being the parent: CH₃OC₂H₅ methoxyethane; C₂H₅OC₂H₅ ethoxyethane; C₆H₅OCH₃ methoxybenzene (anisole).

slides.narration: In an ether the oxygen atom is sp three hybridised with two lone pairs, like the oxygen in an alcohol, but the two bulky alkyl groups push each other apart, so the angle is about one hundred and twelve degrees. Ethers are named as alkoxy alkanes: the smaller group becomes the alkoxy prefix and the larger group is the parent. Diethyl ether is ethoxyethane and anisole is methoxybenzene.

slides.heading: Williamson’s synthesis
slides.body_md: An **alkoxide** (or phenoxide) reacts with a **primary alkyl halide** by **SN2**: R–O⁻Na⁺ + R′–X → R–O–R′ + NaX. With secondary and especially tertiary halides, the strongly basic alkoxide causes **elimination**, so the bulky group must be on the alkoxide. Aryl halides cannot be used (unreactive).

visual.alt: Table of Williamson choices

slides.narration: Williamson’s synthesis is the most general way to make ethers. An alkoxide ion attacks a primary alkyl halide from the back and pushes out the halide. If the halide is tertiary, the alkoxide acts as a base instead and an alkene forms. So, to make an ether with a tertiary group, put the tertiary group on the alkoxide. For an aryl ether, use the phenoxide and an alkyl halide.

slides.heading: Worked example: planning a Williamson synthesis
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Choose reactants for (a) 2-methoxypropane, (b) 2-ethoxy-2-methylbutane and (c) 1-methoxy-4-methylbenzene.

**(a)** Sodium propan-2-oxide + iodomethane: $\ce{(CH3)2CHONa + CH3I -> (CH3)2CHOCH3 + NaI}$.

**(b)** Sodium 2-methylbutan-2-oxide + bromoethane (the tertiary group on the alkoxide).

**(c)** Sodium 4-methylphenoxide + iodomethane.

visual.alt: Table of reactants for Williamson syntheses

slides.narration: Look at the two groups on oxygen and put the more hindered one on the alkoxide, leaving the halide as primary or methyl as possible. For two-methoxypropane, use sodium isopropoxide and iodomethane. For the tertiary ether, the tertiary group must be the alkoxide and bromoethane the halide. For an aryl methyl ether, use the sodium phenoxide and iodomethane.

slides.heading: Physical properties
slides.body_md: Ethers have **no O–H**, so they cannot hydrogen-bond with each other: b.p. close to alkanes of similar mass and much lower than alcohols. They can accept hydrogen bonds from water, so lower ethers are about as soluble in water as alcohols of similar size. Ethoxyethane is volatile, highly **flammable**, and a good **solvent** for organic compounds.

visual.alt: Table of boiling points

slides.narration: Ether molecules have no hydrogen on oxygen, so they cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other, and their boiling points are close to those of alkanes. But the ether oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond from water, so small ethers dissolve in water about as well as alcohols of similar size. Ethoxyethane is very volatile and catches fire easily, so it must be kept away from flames.

slides.heading: Quick check: Williamson synthesis
slides.body_md: Choose the reactants for preparing an ether.
slides.narration: Quick check. The alkyl halide should be primary; any tertiary group belongs on the alkoxide.

slides.heading: Reactions with chlorine, oxygen and PCl₅
slides.body_md: **Chlorine:** in the dark, α-hydrogens are substituted (1-chloroethoxyethane); in light, all H are replaced (perchlorodiethyl ether). **Oxygen:** on standing in air and light, ethers form **peroxides**, which are explosive on distillation; they are detected with FeSO₄ + KSCN (red colour) and removed by shaking with acidified FeSO₄. **PCl₅:** splits ethers into two chloroalkanes.

visual.alt: Table of reactions of ethers with chlorine, oxygen and PCl₅

slides.narration: Ethers are fairly unreactive, which is why they make good solvents, but they do have some reactions. Chlorine substitutes hydrogens next to the oxygen in the dark, and replaces all of them in light. On standing in air and light, ethers slowly form peroxides, which can explode when the ether is distilled, so old ether is tested and treated with iron two sulphate first. Phosphorus pentachloride splits ethers into chloroalkanes.

slides.heading: Cleavage by hydrogen iodide
slides.body_md: Cold HI (1 mol): R–O–R′ → R–I + R′–OH; the **smaller** alkyl group gives the iodide (SN2), but a **tertiary** group gives the iodide (SN1). Hot excess HI: both groups → alkyl iodides. **Aryl alkyl ethers** always give **phenol + alkyl iodide** (the Ar–O bond does not break).

visual.alt: Table of products of ether cleavage by HI

slides.narration: Hydrogen iodide first protonates the ether oxygen. Then iodide attacks a carbon. With methyl and primary groups this is an S N two attack on the less hindered carbon, so the smaller group becomes the iodide. With a tertiary group, a stable carbocation forms and picks up iodide. With aryl ethers, the aryl–oxygen bond has partial double-bond character and never breaks, so phenol is always formed.

slides.heading: Worked example: products of cleavage
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Give the products with one equivalent of HI: (a) 1-methoxybutane; (b) 2-ethoxy-2-methylpropane; (c) methoxybenzene; (d) ethoxyethane with excess hot HI.

**(a)** Iodomethane + butan-1-ol (SN2 at methyl).

**(b)** 2-Iodo-2-methylpropane + ethanol (SN1 at the tertiary carbon).

**(c)** Phenol + iodomethane.

**(d)** Iodoethane only (2 mol) + water.

visual.alt: Table of cleavage products

slides.narration: Identify the two groups on oxygen. Methyl and primary groups react by S N two, so iodide attacks the methyl carbon and butan-one-ol is released. A tertiary group forms a carbocation, so it becomes two-iodo-two-methylpropane and ethanol is released. Methoxybenzene gives phenol and iodomethane. With hot excess hydrogen iodide, the ethanol formed is also converted, so only iodoethane remains.

slides.heading: Quick check: cleavage by HI
slides.body_md: Predict the products of cleaving an ether with HI.
slides.narration: Quick check. Smaller group or tertiary group becomes the iodide; aryl ethers always give phenol.

slides.heading: Anisole: preparation and electrophilic substitution
slides.body_md: **Preparation** (Williamson): sodium phenoxide + iodomethane (or dimethyl sulphate). The **–OCH₃** group activates the ring (+R) and directs **ortho/para**; para usually predominates.

visual.alt: Table of electrophilic substitution of anisole

slides.narration: Anisole is made by Williamson’s synthesis from sodium phenoxide and iodomethane. Its methoxy group pushes electrons into the ring, so anisole is more reactive than benzene and is substituted at ortho and para positions. Bromine reacts even without a catalyst, in ethanoic acid. Nitration and Friedel–Crafts alkylation and acylation give mainly the para products.

slides.heading: Worked example: products from anisole
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Give the major product of anisole with (a) Br₂ in ethanoic acid; (b) conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄; (c) CH₃COCl/AlCl₃; (d) excess HI. Why is para favoured over ortho in (a)–(c)?

**(a)** 1-Bromo-4-methoxybenzene. **(b)** 1-Methoxy-4-nitrobenzene. **(c)** 1-(4-Methoxyphenyl)ethan-1-one. **(d)** Phenol + iodomethane.

The –OCH₃ group hinders the adjacent ortho positions, so para substitution is preferred.

visual.alt: Table of anisole products

slides.narration: All three electrophilic substitutions go mainly para to the methoxy group, because the methoxy group crowds the neighbouring ortho positions. Bromination gives four-bromoanisole, nitration four-nitroanisole and acylation four-methoxyacetophenone. Hydrogen iodide is different: it attacks the ether linkage itself and gives phenol and iodomethane.

slides.heading: Uses of ethers
slides.body_md: Ethoxyethane: solvent for oils, fats, resins and Grignard reactions; formerly a general anaesthetic. Methoxymethane: refrigerant and aerosol propellant. Anisole: perfumes and as an intermediate. Ethers in general: inert reaction media.

visual.alt: Table of uses of ethers

slides.narration: Ethoxyethane is an excellent solvent for fats, oils and resins, and it is the classic solvent for Grignard reactions because it is unreactive and dissolves the reagents. It was once used as a general anaesthetic. Methoxymethane is used as a refrigerant and aerosol propellant, and anisole is used in perfumes and as a starting material for other compounds.

slides.heading: Quick check: anisole
slides.body_md: Predict a product of electrophilic substitution of anisole.
slides.narration: Quick check. The methoxy group activates the ring and directs ortho and para, mainly para.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Ether O sp³, C–O–C ≈ 111.7°; alkoxyalkane names.
Williamson: RONa + primary R′X (SN2); tertiary group on the alkoxide; aryl group on the phenoxide.
B.p. like alkanes (no H-bonds between molecules); soluble like alcohols (accept H-bonds).
Cl₂ (dark: α-substitution; light: perchloro); O₂ → explosive peroxides; PCl₅ → 2RCl.
HI: smaller or tertiary group → iodide; aryl ethers → phenol + RI.
Anisole: o/p activating; bromination, nitration, Friedel–Crafts give mainly para products.

visual.alt: Summary table of HI cleavage

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Ethers are made by Williamson’s synthesis from an alkoxide and a primary halide. They boil like alkanes but dissolve like alcohols. They react with chlorine, slowly form explosive peroxides in air, and are split by phosphorus pentachloride and hydrogen iodide, with predictable products. Anisole is activated towards ortho and para substitution.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2
bullets: In Williamson questions, explain why the halide must be primary.
For HI cleavage, state the mechanism (SN1 or SN2) behind your choice.
Mention peroxide hazards when asked about storing or distilling ethers.
Anisole bromination needs no Lewis acid.

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 2 and fixes

slides.narration: Final tips. In Williamson questions, explain why the halide should be primary. In cleavage questions, give the mechanism that decides which group becomes the iodide. Mention peroxides when asked about the hazards of ethers. And remember that anisole is so reactive that bromination needs no catalyst.

Mono-, di-, trihydric phenols: phenol; cresols (methylphenols); catechol (1,2-), resorcinol (1,3-), quinol (1,4-diol); pyrogallol (1,2,3-triol).

sections.heading: 3. Electrophilic substitution, named reactions, tests and uses
sections.body_md:
–OH activates (+R), o/p directing. Br₂(aq) → **2,4,6-tribromophenol** (white ppt); Br₂/CS₂, 273 K → 4- (and 2-) bromophenol. Dilute HNO₃ → 2- and 4-nitrophenol; conc. HNO₃ → **picric acid**. Conc. H₂SO₄: 2-sulphonic acid at about 290 K, 4- at about 373 K.

**Kolbe:** C₆H₅ONa + CO₂ (400 K, 4–7 atm), H⁺ → **salicylic acid**. **Reimer–Tiemann:** CHCl₃ + NaOH (via :CCl₂), H⁺ → **salicylaldehyde**.

**Tests:** neutral FeCl₃ → violet; azo dye with benzenediazonium chloride (alkaline, cold) → orange 4-hydroxyazobenzene; bromine water → white ppt. **Uses:** antiseptics, Bakelite, aspirin, dyes, picric acid.

sections.heading: 4. Aliphatic ethers
sections.body_md:
O sp³; C–O–C ≈ 111.7°; named as alkoxyalkanes (2-ethoxypropane). **Williamson:** RONa + primary R′X (SN2); tertiary groups go on the alkoxide (tertiary halides eliminate). Also 2ROH → ROR (conc. H₂SO₄, 413 K).

**Preparation:** C₆H₅ONa + CH₃I → C₆H₅OCH₃ + NaI. –OCH₃ activates (+R), o/p directing, para major: Br₂ in ethanoic acid (no catalyst) → 4-bromoanisole; HNO₃/H₂SO₄ → 4-nitroanisole; CH₃Cl/AlCl₃ → 4-methylanisole; CH₃COCl/AlCl₃ → 4-methoxyacetophenone. **HI** → phenol + CH₃I (aryl C–O does not break).

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying phenol reacts with NaHCO₃.
- Giving monobromophenol for bromine water (it is 2,4,6-tribromophenol).
- Using a tertiary halide in Williamson’s synthesis.
- Writing iodobenzene as a product of anisole + HI.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Acidity (2 marks): resonance structures of phenoxide; substituent effects.
- Named reactions (1–2 marks): reagents, conditions and product names.
- Ether cleavage (1–2 marks): products with the mechanism that decides them.

answer.model_answer_md: Loss of H⁺ from phenol gives the phenoxide ion, in which the negative charge is delocalised from oxygen onto the ortho and para carbons of the ring (several resonance structures), stabilising the ion. questions.stem_md: Arrange 2,4-dinitrophenol, phenol, 4-methylphenol and 3-nitrophenol in order of increasing acid strength, and explain the order.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write equations for preparing phenol from (i) sodium benzenesulphonate and (ii) benzenediazonium chloride. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) $\ce{C6H5SO3Na + 2NaOH ->[573 K] C6H5ONa + Na2SO3 + H2O}$, then $\ce{C6H5ONa + HCl -> C6H5OH + NaCl}$. (ii) $\ce{C6H5N2Cl + H2O ->[warm] C6H5OH + N2 + HCl}$.

(b) The phenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation of the negative charge over the oxygen and the ortho and para carbons. A 4-NO₂ group withdraws electrons (−R, −I) and delocalises the charge further onto its oxygens, increasing acidity; a 4-CH₃ group releases electrons (+I, hyperconjugation), destabilising the ion and decreasing acidity.

(c) $\ce{2C6H5OH + 2Na -> 2C6H5ONa + H2}$; $\ce{C6H5OH + Zn -> C6H6 + ZnO}$.

questions.solution_md: Two preparations; resonance and substituents; Na and Zn.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Compare the bromination of phenol in water and in carbon disulphide, and explain the difference. [1½]

(b) Write equations for the Kolbe and Reimer–Tiemann reactions. [2]

(c) Give two tests that distinguish phenol from ethanol. [1½]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In water: 2,4,6-tribromophenol (white precipitate) at once. In CS₂ at 273 K: mainly 4-bromophenol with some 2-bromophenol. In water phenol partly ionises to the strongly activating phenoxide ion and Br₂ is polarised; in non-polar CS₂ neither happens, so substitution is milder.

(b) Kolbe: $\ce{C6H5ONa + CO2 ->[400 K, 4-7 atm] HOC6H4COONa}$, then H⁺ → salicylic acid. Reimer–Tiemann: $\ce{C6H5OH + CHCl3 + 3NaOH -> HOC6H4CHO + 3NaCl + 2H2O}$ (via the phenoxide; acidify) → salicylaldehyde.

(c) Neutral FeCl₃: violet with phenol, none with ethanol. Bromine water: white precipitate with phenol only. (Or: phenol dissolves in NaOH; azo dye test.)

questions.solution_md: Tribromo vs mono; Kolbe and RT; FeCl₃ and Br₂ water.

(b) (i) Iodomethane + butan-1-ol (SN2 at the methyl carbon). (ii) 2-Iodo-2-methylpropane + ethanol (SN1 via the tertiary carbocation).

(c) In air and light ethers slowly form explosive peroxides.

answer.model_answer_md:

(b) $\ce{C6H5OCH3 + Br2 ->[CH3COOH] BrC6H4OCH3 + HBr}$: 4-bromoanisole. $\ce{C6H5OCH3 + HNO3 ->[H2SO4] O2NC6H4OCH3 + H2O}$: 4-nitroanisole. $\ce{C6H5OCH3 + CH3COCl ->[AlCl3] CH3COC6H4OCH3 + HCl}$: 4-methoxyacetophenone (2-isomers minor).

(c) $\ce{C6H5OCH3 + HI -> C6H5OH + CH3I}$: phenol and iodomethane.

questions.solution_md: Williamson; three para products; phenol + CH₃I.

questions.stem_md:
How would you carry out the following conversions? Give reagents and conditions. [1 each]

(a) Phenol to anisole

(b) Phenol to salicylaldehyde

(c) Phenol to benzene
